results.title: The Measurement Error Elephant in the Room: Challenges and Solutions to Measurement Error in Epidemiology - PMC
results.content: This review offers a straightforward guide to common problems caused by measurement error in research studies and a review of several accessible bias-correction methods for epidemiologists and data analysts. Although most correction methods require criterion validation including a gold standard, there are also ways to evaluate the impact of measurement error and potentially correct for it without such data. **Keywords:** bias correction, epidemiologic methods, epidemiologic review, measurement error, sensitivity analyses. As discussed in the following sections, most methods that correct for measurement error require validation data—ideally internal validation data, which are collected within the parent study, but with certain assumptions, validation data can be external to the study—to quantify the error and appropriately correct for it. For example, Carroll et al (1) considered 2 different departures: one where *A\** is no longer unbiased for *A,* and a second where *A\** contains differential measurement error. Some methods for measurement error correction require a validation data set to impute missing gold standard values, whereas others need validation data to estimate the error variance or a calibration parameter. Regression calibration (RC) is a clever and intuitive method suitable for nondifferential independent measurement error that corrects point and variance estimates for bias due to measurement error in 1 or more continuous covariates (but not the outcome) with a continuous or dichotomous outcome (39). A further advantage is that, because the measurement error correction is performed at the data level rather than correcting the estimated measure of association, MIME’s application is not limited to specific models or data types. Given that often analysts will encounter studies in which validation data are not available, sensitivity analysis methods that assess the potential or plausible impact of measurement error may be the most useful tools in the measurement error toolbox. Even without internal validation data, there are tools to help quantify the effect of measurement error and even correct it. Regression calibration method for correcting measurement-error bias in nutritional epidemiology. Estimation and inference for logistic regression with covariate misclassification and measurement error in main study/validation study designs. A method for sensitivity analysis to assess the effects of measurement error in multiple exposure variables using external validation data.

results.title: modeling - Additive Error or Multiplicative Error? - Cross Validated
results.content: In my field there is a commonly used model of the form: $$P\_t = P\_o(V\_t)^\alpha$$ When people fit the model to data they usually linearise it and fit the following $$\log(P\_t) = \log(P\_o) + \alpha \log(V\_t) + \epsilon$$ I read somewhere that because of noise in the signal the actual model should be $$P\_t = P\_o(V\_t)^\alpha + \epsilon$$ and this cannot be linearised as above. 2015-02-19 17:14:32 +00:00 Commented Feb 19, 2015 at 17:14 * $\begingroup$ You've flagged your question with "measurement error" and the +e in the 3rd equation would seem to be due to additive measurement error in addition to multiplicative stochastic/random variation in the response, something like P\*(V^alpha)\*exp(e). Measurement error models (aka "error in variables" models) often require a kind of two-step process, which in your case might require separate validation data to characterize the additive error due to "noise", in which case there might not be a need to linearise the equation. 2015-02-20 03:52:36 +00:00 Commented Feb 20, 2015 at 3:52 ## 1 Answer 1 Which model is appropriate depends on how variation around the mean comes into the observations. With the log-linear model, where linear regression is used: $\log(P\_t)=log(P\_o)+α\log(V\_t)+ϵ$ the OLS regression model assumes constant log-scale variance, and if that's the case, then the original data will show an increasing spread about the mean as the mean increases. On the other hand, this sort of model: $P\_t=P\_o(V\_t)^α+ϵ$ is generally fitted by nonlinear least squares, and again, if constant variance (the default for NLS) is fitted, then the spread about the mean should be constant. [You may have the visual impression that the spread is decreasing with increasing mean in the last image; that's actually an illusion caused by the increasing slope - we tend to judge the spread orthogonal to the curve rather than vertically so we get a distorted impression.] If you have nearly constant spread on either the original or the log scale, that might suggest which of the two models to fit, not because it proves it's additive or multiplicative, but because it leads to an appropriate description of the spread as well as the mean.

results.title: What's the difference between a multiplicative model and an additive model with the variable converted to log? - Quora
results.content: What's the difference between a multiplicative model and an additive model with the variable converted to log? A multiplicative model and an additive model with the variable converted to log are closely related but not identical. * Additive-on-log model (log-linear): log y = log a + b \* log x + u, where u = log ε is an additive error on the log scale. A multiplicative model and an additive model with the variable converted to log are closely related but not identical. * Additive-on-log model (log-linear): log y = log a + b \* log x + u, where u = log ε is an additive error on the log scale. - In a literal multiplicative model on original scale, b also plays the elasticity role but converting back from log estimates may require bias correction (see point 4). Multiplicative relationships with zeros or negatives need alternative approaches (e.g., generalized linear models with log link, additive models on original scale, or two-part models). - Consider GLM with log link (E[y|x] = exp(β0 + β1 log x)) if you want multiplicative mean structure but model errors on original scale (Poisson/Gamma families support multiplicative mean with different variance assumptions).
